Simul Justus
SIM-ool YOOS-toos
Latin theological formula (Reformation soteriology)
Latin simul (simultaneously, at the same time) combined with justus (just, righteous) and peccator (sinner); the full phrase is simul justus et peccator — simultaneously justified and sinner; coined by Luther in his Lectures on Romans (1515–1516) to name the paradox at the heart of Reformed soteriology: the regenerate soul is at once fully righteous in Christ's imputed obedience and still indwelling sin in the flesh

Biblical Definition

The Reformation formula simul justus et peccator — simultaneously justified and sinner — captures the defining paradox of the regenerate soul in this age. The believer stands before God perfectly righteous in Christ through imputed righteousness (justification complete and irreversible), while indwelling sin remains active in the flesh (sanctification ongoing and incomplete). These two realities coexist in the same person at the same moment: no condemnation, yet the warfare of Romans 7 persists. Paul's double statement — “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.” (Rom 7:25) — is not pre-conversion autobiography; it is the mature apostle's honest confession. The formula guards against two opposite errors. First, perfectionism: the claim that regeneration eradicates indwelling sin in this life. John's rebuke stands: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” (1 John 1:8). Second, antinomian despair: the false conclusion that sin's persistence means justification is threatened. Romans 8:1 counters: “There is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.” Justification is an objective forensic verdict grounded in Christ's finished obedience, imputed to faith — it does not fluctuate with moral performance. Sanctification is the ongoing, Spirit-driven mortification of remaining sin. Glorification will finally close the gap. Until that day, the saint lives simul: simultaneously in both realities, groaning in hope.

Webster 1828 Definition

SIMUL JUSTUS: Latin Reformation formula meaning “simultaneously justified and sinner” (simul justus et peccator); names the paradox that the regenerate believer is at once fully righteous in Christ by imputation and still afflicted by indwelling sin, with justification complete and sanctification ongoing until glorification.

SIMUL JUSTUS ET PECCATOR. Latin. Simultaneously justified and sinner. The Reformation formula coined by Luther (Lectures on Romans, 1515–1516) to describe the permanent soteriological condition of the regenerate soul in this age.

The formula holds in tension two realities that never collapse into each other: (1) the forensic verdict of justification, by which God declares the sinner righteous on the basis of Christ's imputed active and passive obedience — a verdict rendered once, fully, and irrevocably; and (2) the continuing presence of indwelling sin (peccatum manens) in the regenerate person's flesh, against which the Spirit wages war throughout the Christian life.

The simul is an eschatological statement: the believer inhabits two ages at once. The old age persists in the flesh; the new age has arrived in the Spirit. Glorification will end the simul by completing the believer's conformity to Christ.

Confessional basis: 1689 LBCF 13 (Of Sanctification) holds that sanctification “is imperfect in this life; there abideth still some remnants of corruption in every part” while 1689 LBCF 11 (Of Justification) grounds the verdict entirely in Christ's imputed obedience.

Key Scripture

Rom 7:25 — "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin."

Rom 8:1 — "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

Gal 2:20 — "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me."

1 John 1:8 — "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."

Modern Corruption

Roman Catholicism conflates justification with sanctification, denying the forensic verdict; Wesleyan perfectionism denies remaining indwelling sin; both destroy the simul by different routes and make assurance unavailable.

expand to see more

The Council of Trent (1547, Decree on Justification, Canon 11) anathematized the forensic understanding of justification, redefining it as the process of inner moral renewal rather than a declarative verdict. On this scheme the simul is impossible: one cannot be simultaneously justified while still a sinner, because justification remains incomplete until the sinner has been actually made righteous in practice. Assurance of salvation becomes unavailable this side of death, and the conscience is bound to the confessional rather than to Christ's finished obedience. Vatican II did not revoke Trent; the Roman system continues to hold that justifying grace is infused rather than imputed, and the forensic verdict remains rejected.

Wesleyan-Holiness theology introduced “entire sanctification” — the claim that the Spirit can fully eradicate indwelling sin in this life, rendering the believer wholly sanctified through a crisis “second blessing.” This collapses the simul at the upper end: the entirely sanctified soul is no longer “also sinner.” But Scripture permanently checks all such claims. John writes without qualification: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” (1 John 1:8). The apostle does not mark an era of Christian life at which this ceases to apply. Reformed theology reads the Spirit's progressive sanctification as lifelong warfare (Gal 5:16–17; Rom 8:13) that ends only at glorification, never at an attained crisis-experience.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin simul (at the same time) + justus (righteous) + et (and) + peccator (sinner); the full phrase coined by Luther (1515–1516) as an exegetical summary of Paul's argument in Romans 7–8; the most compact Reformed statement of the paradox of regeneration.

expand to see more

Latin simul — at the same time, simultaneously; the word insists on simultaneity rather than sequence: not “first justified, then sinner” nor “sinner until no longer justified” but both at once, in the same person, in the same moment throughout the present age

Latin justus — just, righteous; in the Reformation context specifically forensically righteous by imputation — the accused declared righteous by a judicial act of God rather than made righteous by infused virtue; the righteousness is Christ's own, credited to the believer's account by faith

Latin peccator — sinner; in the Augustinian and Reformation tradition, one whose nature retains the corruption of original sin even after regeneration; the regenerate peccator wars against remaining sin (peccatum manens) but does not overcome it completely in this life

Latin et — and; the joining conjunction is the heart of the formula: it holds two realities together rather than resolving the tension by collapsing one into the other; the et refuses both perfectionism and antinomian despair

Martin Luther, Lectures on Romans (1515–1516) — the classroom lectures in which Luther forged the phrase as an exegetical summary of Paul's argument; it became one of the most compact formulas of Reformation soteriology and the doctrinal foundation for the Reformed account of the Christian life

Usage

"Reformed preaching on Romans 7 must hold the simul with pastoral precision: the warfare of the flesh is real and unending in this life, and honest struggle with sin is not evidence of false conversion but the normal condition of the genuine saint. Antinomian despair — “I must not be saved because I still struggle” — contradicts the formula directly. The pastor's task is to distinguish the forensic verdict (no condemnation, Rom 8:1) from the ongoing experience (groaning under indwelling sin, Rom 7:24) without collapsing either into the other."

"The formula distinguishes two courtrooms. In the court of God, the believer stands justified — declared righteous on the basis of Christ's imputed obedience, a verdict already rendered and never reversed. In the court of experience, battle with remaining sin continues in the same person who stands righteous before God (Rom 7:23). These two courts must never be confused: the inner state of the struggling believer does not modify the forensic standing, and the forensic standing does not eliminate the reality of the inner struggle. Both are true at once."

"The simul is the doctrinal foundation for the Reformation's recovery of assurance. Because justification is a complete forensic act rather than a process dependent on the believer's moral progress, assurance is possible — not as presumption (which forgets the peccator) but as confidence in Christ's finished work (which grasps the justus). The 1689 LBCF's chapter on assurance (18) grounds it precisely here: assurance rests on the divine promises and the work of the Spirit, not on the believer's subjective moral achievement."
